1.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the four dimensions of business language is/are true?
o: Product answers “What?” and can be a digital service.
Participants covers only people employed by the business.
Purpose answers “Why?” and includes mission, vision and strategic goals.
Participants answers “Who?” and can include AI agents.
Process answers “What?” and describes the goods delivered.
1.e: Purpose = Why, Participants = Who, Process = How, Product = What.
w: True: Product covers physical or digital goods and services, or hybrids, so a digital service qualifies.
False: Participants include external parties such as customers and suppliers, and systems, not only internal staff.
True: Purpose is the business's North Star: it states why the business exists and what it is trying to achieve.
True: Participants covers every stakeholder, team, customer and system, and the course now extends this to AI agents.
False: Process answers “How?”: it is the workflow that connects participants. What is delivered belongs to Product.

1.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the course journey is/are true?
o: Solve specifies IT functional and non-functional requirements.
Model comes before Analyse.
Analyse produces issues and recommendations.
Innovate comes before Solve.
Innovate is the last chapter.
1.e: The order is Model, Analyse, Solve, Innovate.
w: True: Solve turns the To-Be models into requirements and solutioning models such as use case, function, architecture, risk and cost.
True: Analyse studies the As-Is models, so those models must be built first.
True: Analysis of the As-Is yields issues and recommendations, and the To-Be state is then modelled.
False: Innovate is the last chapter; it feeds technology and business-model ideas into the To-Be designs.
True: Innovation extends the To-Be after the process is understood and the solution specified.

1.q: Which of the following statement(s) about a business's Purpose is/are true?
o: A single North Star Metric can measure the value it creates.
It is the same dimension as Participants.
It describes the workflows that deliver value.
It is described by mission, vision and strategic goals.
It is the reason a business exists: to create value.
w: True: One metric that measures value gives the whole organisation a shared target.
False: Participants is a separate dimension answering Who?; Purpose answers Why?.
False: Workflows belong to the Process dimension; Purpose is about why the business exists.
True: These three express why the business exists and where it is heading.
True: Creating value is the heart of Purpose, which is why it is called the North Star.

1.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the Product dimension is/are true?
o: It covers digital services.
It can be a hybrid of goods and services.
It describes the stakeholders who deliver value.
It describes how work flows between roles.
It covers physical goods.
w: True: Digital services, such as a mobile app, are product kinds too.
True: Hybrids are named explicitly in the definition.
False: Stakeholders are the Participants dimension; Product is what they deliver.
False: That is the Process dimension, which answers How?.
True: Physical goods are one of the kinds of product named in the dimension.

2.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the levels of alignment is/are true?
o: The two levels have the same scope.
Enterprise Alignment covers the whole organisation.
Project Alignment is delivered through the Business Process Engineering Methodology.
Enterprise Alignment is delivered through the Business Process Engineering Methodology.
Project Alignment concerns the whole organisation.
w: False: One spans the whole organisation and the other a single solution, so their scope differs.
True: It aligns objectives, processes, information, applications and technology across the entire organisation.
True: That methodology aligns one specific IT solution with the business.
False: Enterprise Alignment is delivered through Enterprise Architecture; the methodology belongs to project alignment.
False: Project Alignment concerns one IT solution; whole-organisation scope is Enterprise Alignment.

2.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the BPM implementation cycle is/are true?
o: It ends once the solution is implemented.
Monitor & Optimise feeds back into the cycle.
It starts with Discover.
Discover produces the final To-Be design.
Design Solution corresponds to Solve.
2.e: Discover, Model & Analyse, Design Solution, Implement Solution, Monitor & Optimise.
w: False: The cycle keeps turning for as long as the organisation exists; implementation is only one phase.
True: BPM is an ongoing effort, so results of monitoring start the next round.
True: Discover understands the current state and sets context before any modelling.
False: Discover only sets context and scope; the To-Be is designed after modelling and analysis.
True: Solve is where the IT solution is specified, which is the design step of the cycle.

2.q: Which of the following statement(s) about mission, vision and objectives is/are true?
o: A vision describes the future the company aspires to.
A business objective is measurable and time-bound.
A mission is abstract and a vision is concrete.
A vision statement is measurable and time-bound.
A mission describes what the company does now.
2.e: Mission = now; vision = future; objective = measurable.
w: True: It is broad and inspirational, a long-term goal.
True: Objectives carry numbers and deadlines, which later lets performance goals be tested.
False: It is the reverse: the mission is concrete and specific, the vision abstract and broad.
False: Measurable, time-bound statements are objectives; a vision is directional.
True: It states current purpose and guides day-to-day decisions.

2.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the Discover phase is/are true?
o: It collects input from process owners only.
Incomplete documentation is mitigated by observing and interviewing.
Its outputs include a list of in-scope processes.
It is deliberately shallow and sets context.
It produces simulation results for To-Be alternatives.
w: False: It also gathers requirements from end users, customers and subject matter experts.
True: Documents may be outdated, so people and practice are checked directly.
True: It also produces stakeholder roles, current-state documentation, requirements and a baseline assessment.
True: Detailed elicitation is a separate, deeper step that follows it.
False: Simulation belongs to dynamic analysis, much later in the cycle.

3.q: Which of the following statement(s) about a business process is/are true?
o: It is a one-off series of activities.
It has performance indicators with measurable objectives.
It is initiated by one or more business events.
An activity can be decomposed into further sub-processes.
It transforms inputs into outputs using resources.
w: False: The course definition says repeatable; one-off work is a project.
True: KPIs make the process's performance evaluable.
True: An event, such as a customer arriving, triggers the process.
False: An activity is the atomic unit; it is a sub-process that decomposes further.
True: Guidance and resources, human or system, are part of the unpacked definition.

3.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the six questions about a business is/are true?
o: How? covers organisation structure.
Why? covers business rules.
Who? covers people and systems.
What? covers raw materials, data and products.
Where? covers location, including online and face-to-face.
3.e: What, How, Why, When, Who, Where.
w: False: Organisation structure belongs to Who?; How? is workflow and process flow.
False: Rules sit under When?; Why? is business strategy, objectives and KPIs.
True: Both organisation structure and IT infrastructure are included.
True: It addresses inputs, outputs and what the business handles.
True: Channels such as dine-in, takeaway and delivery fall here.

3.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the components of a business process is/are true?
o: A process needs no resources.
Business documents such as an invoice are involved.
A process may be divided into sub-processes and activities.
A process cannot have performance indicators.
Resources include humans and systems.
w: False: Transforming inputs to outputs requires resources, by definition.
True: They appear as work products that flow through the process.
True: Decomposition is part of the structure.
False: A defined set of KPIs is one of its key components.
True: Applications count as resources alongside people.

3.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the three lenses of a process model is/are true?
o: The Workflow lens answers Who?.
The Data lens answers What?.
The Workflow lens answers How?.
The Data lens answers How?.
The Resources lens answers Who?.
3.e: Resources = Who, Workflow = How, Data = What.
w: False: Who? belongs to the Resources lens; Workflow is the sequence of steps.
True: It captures what goes in and what comes out.
True: It captures the ordered steps.
False: How? belongs to the Workflow lens; Data is inputs and outputs.
True: It covers the people and systems that perform the work.

4.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the Organisation Model is/are true?
o: A Functional Role exists only for the length of one workflow.
A Process Role may not appear on the org chart.
It shows where stakeholders are geographically.
It shows roles and reporting structures.
It helps determine access control for an IT solution.
w: False: That describes a Process Role; a Functional Role is an organisational title such as Salesclerk.
True: It exists because a process needs it, such as a Requester.
False: Geography is the Location Model; the Organisation Model shows structure.
True: It answers who reports to whom and is informally called People Politics.
True: Knowing who holds which role shows who the end-users are and what each may access.

4.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the Location Model is/are true?
o: It informs IT solution deployment decisions.
It shows the sequence of activities.
Transactions across time zones should use local time.
It helps identify location-specific needs such as language.
It shows how stakeholders are distributed across physical locations.
w: True: Infrastructure and cost vary by location, which affects deployment.
False: Sequence is shown by the Process Workflow Model.
False: They should use GMT so every site refers to the same instant.
True: Local culture and government policy also differ by site.
True: That is its purpose, giving a geographic view of the same stakeholders.

4.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the Resource Model is/are true?
o: A paid third-party cloud system is external.
A resource belongs in it only if it participates in the process.
Internal means the resource is used by employees.
It categorises resources as internal or external.
A resource the company owns but the process never touches is left out.
w: True: Internal and external track who controls the resource, not who pays for it.
True: A system the company owns but the process never touches is left out.
False: Internal means you manage the resource, whoever uses it.
True: It also separates human resources from technology.
True: Only resources that participate in the process belong in the model.

4.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the seven process-model views is/are true?
o: Collaboration and Process Package are among them.
Organisation, Location and Resource are among them.
Only five views exist.
All seven must always be built.
Process Workflow and Business Rules are among them.
w: True: They are the two views not studied in depth.
True: They are the first three models studied.
False: Seven views exist; five of them are studied.
False: You decide which model best tells your story; modelling is resource-intensive.
True: They complete the five models studied.

5.q: Which of the following statement(s) about activity types is/are true?
o: Parallel is a third activity type.
An interactive activity is done by a human using a system.
A manual activity is done by humans unaided by systems.
An interactive activity belongs in the system's lane.
An automated activity is done entirely by a system.
w: False: Parallel is a gateway behaviour; the activity types are manual, interactive and automated.
True: It stays in the human's lane because the human performs it.
True: No system is touched, so it sits in the human's lane.
False: The lane follows who performs the activity, and here a human performs it.
True: No human is involved, so it sits in the system's lane.

5.q: Which of the following statement(s) about BPMN symbols is/are true?
o: A diamond with a plus shows parallel activities.
A solid arrow is a transition.
A circle is a swimlane.
A dashed arrow links a work product to an activity.
A diamond is always a decision.
w: True: Its branches run at the same time rather than exclusively.
True: It is the sequence flow from one element to the next.
False: A circle is a business event; a swimlane is a horizontal band.
True: It is an association, for example to a document or data object.
False: A merge can also be a diamond, so decisions and merges are told apart by counting flows.

5.q: Which of the following statement(s) about business rules is/are true?
o: A rule set needs no name.
They attach to decision gateways.
They are written in plain natural language.
They may apply to manual as well as automated activities.
They follow IF … THEN … with AND/OR and sometimes ELSE.
w: False: A rule set has a Name field, plus the activity using it, a description and related rule sets.
False: They attach to the activity that evaluates the condition; the gateway only shows that a branch exists.
True: Not pseudocode or formal grammar, and they use business vocabulary.
True: Both kinds of activity can need documented rules.
True: Conditions chain with AND/OR and lead to a consequence.

5.q: Which of the following statement(s) about a swimlane is/are true?
o: Every stakeholder in the Resource Model gets a lane.
It groups the activities performed by one Business Participant.
A stakeholder who only receives a document gets a lane.
A lane represents the tools used.
A stakeholder needs an actual activity to earn a lane.
w: False: Only those who perform an activity in this process do.
True: The label at the left names the participant who owns the lane.
False: A lane needs a performed activity; merely receiving something does not earn one.
False: A lane represents who performs the work, not which tool is touched.
True: Being a stakeholder in another model is not enough.

6.q: Which of the following statement(s) about reading a BPMN diagram is/are true?
o: A decision has several labelled exits.
A merge has several entries and one exit.
A merge does not count as a decision box.
Every diamond counts as a decision.
A decision and a merge can share the same exclusive-gateway marker.
w: True: Count the flows leaving the diamond.
True: It brings separate paths back together.
True: Only a diamond with several labelled exits is a decision.
False: Merges are not decisions, so a diagram can have more diamonds than decisions.
True: So the number of flows, not the shape, tells them apart.

6.q: Which of the following statement(s) about diagram statistics is/are true?
o: Every diamond is a decision.
Activities, lanes, decisions and start and end points can be counted.
Lanes are counted by the tools used.
Decisions are counted separately from merges.
A lane change is a hand-off between roles.
w: False: Some diamonds are merges.
True: This is a useful sanity check on any diagram you build.
False: Lanes belong to participants, not tools.
True: Only decisions count as decision boxes.
True: These hand-offs are where waiting appears in dynamic analysis.

6.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the order management example is/are true?
o: It includes a timer that drives a loop.
It has four lanes.
It has only one end event.
It has no work products.
It includes a parallel split and join.
w: True: A backorder waits a day and is checked again.
True: Customer, Sales Agent, Sales System and Store Keeper.
False: It has two: one for an invalid order and one for order completion.
False: Work products such as the Sales Order and Purchase Invoice appear in it.
True: Packing and invoicing happen simultaneously.

6.q: Which of the following statement(s) about timing tables with branches is/are true?
o: Only the last gateway's percentage matters.
Times in the table are in hours.
Each step lists its previous step or steps.
A branch can carry a percentage.
Nested branches multiply their probabilities.
6.e: Learn the shape of the table.
w: False: Earlier branches also reduce how often the step occurs.
False: Execution times are given in minutes.
True: That records the order in which steps follow each other.
True: Probabilities annotate the outgoing paths of a gateway.
True: A step after two branches occurs with the joint probability.

7.q: Which of the following statement(s) about static and dynamic analysis is/are true?
o: Dynamic analysis needs no input data.
Dynamic analysis can run a simulation.
Static analysis is more expensive than dynamic analysis.
Static analysis cannot see waiting, queuing or randomness.
Static analysis examines the process without executing it.
w: False: It is only as good as the data fed into the simulation.
True: It can also pilot the process, using real or assumed data.
False: Static analysis is cheap and immediate because it uses documents you already have.
True: That is its blind spot, since nothing is executed.
True: For example, it reviews interview scripts and As-Is models.

7.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the RCI Model is/are true?
o: The impact level uses a 3-point scale.
It includes an Issue Category column.
The root cause should restate the issue.
It includes Business Performance Metrics.
The root cause is the first effect observed.
w: False: It uses a 5-point scale from Very High to Very Low.
True: Categories are Process, System, People, Policy and Others.
False: Repeating the symptom as the root cause explains nothing about why it occurs.
True: They name the metrics the issue affects, and they must be measurable.
False: It is the top-level cause behind the issue, not the first visible effect.

7.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the RCR Model is/are true?
o: Recommendations come from a single source.
Complexity score 5 means Very Easy.
Impact score 5 means Very High.
Complexity score 5 means Very Complex.
It converts the RCI into prioritised recommendations.
w: False: They come from four: domain understanding, technology understanding, industry best practices and experience.
True: The scale is reversed so that a higher number is more attractive.
True: A bigger impact is more attractive.
False: Very Complex is 1; reading the scale backwards is a common mistake.
True: Each recommendation gets a benefit score and an effort score.

7.q: Which of the following statement(s) about static reports is/are true?
o: Utilisation equals required resources divided by resources available.
A static report shows waiting time.
Cost per task converts the weighted time to hours and multiplies by the hourly cost.
Optional tasks are counted at full probability.
Required resources equal annual workload divided by hours per resource.
w: True: It gives the share of capacity used.
False: A static report has no queues, so waiting is invisible to it.
True: Minutes are divided by 60 first.
False: They are weighted by their input factor, which is below 1.
True: This is the step before utilisation.

8.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the four phases of dynamic analysis is/are true?
o: Phase 4 is Impact Analysis.
Phase 2 produces numbers for the As-Is and each To-Be alternative.
Phase 1 establishes performance goals.
Phase 1 is Model and Simulate.
Phase 3 analyses impact on internal and external parties.
w: False: Phase 4 is Final Selection; Impact Analysis is phase 3.
True: It models and simulates each of them.
True: It sets the yardstick against which results are tested.
False: Phase 1 is Establish Performance Goals; simulation is phase 2.
True: It is the last analysis before choosing.

8.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the data collected for simulation is/are true?
o: Decision-point data gives probabilities of paths.
Activity-related data includes how a queue is handled.
Resource-related data includes the cost and number of resources per role.
Resource-related data gives the arrival pattern.
Process-wide data includes the arrival pattern of triggers.
w: True: They come from history or from assumption.
True: It also covers time distribution, cost and resource needs.
True: It also covers work hours and maximum utilisation.
False: Arrival pattern is process-wide data; resource data covers cost, numbers and work hours.
True: It also includes start time and the rate of triggers.

8.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the analysis techniques is/are true?
o: What-if analysis examines only one scenario.
Path analysis examines the paths created by decision points.
Unusual event analysis covers rare events with huge impact.
Bottleneck analysis combines process, resource and activity analysis.
Capacity analysis measures the cost of each activity.
w: False: It compares various possible scenarios.
True: Some tools call them cases or branches.
True: For example, the effect of a flooded warehouse.
True: It finds what causes work to wait.
False: It measures the maximum capacity of the process under defined conditions.

8.q: Which of the following statement(s) about path and what-if analysis is/are true?
o: A path has one start and one end.
The option with the lowest waiting time always wins.
In what-if, find the smallest option that meets the goal, then price it.
Paths should be ranked by expected contribution, share × value.
The path that costs most per case is always the priority.
w: True: That is how the course defines a path.
False: A cheaper option may already meet the goal.
True: The option with the lowest waiting time ignores cost.
True: A rare, expensive path contributes little overall.
False: Its share of cases may be tiny, so its expected contribution is small.

8.q: Which of the following statement(s) about impact analysis and final selection is/are true?
o: Large impacts can rule out an otherwise good alternative.
Simulation always reflects reality perfectly.
The final selection draws on goals, simulation, impact and management decisions.
Impact analysis comes before establishing goals.
Impact is judged as hard or soft and internal or external.
w: True: Feasibility depends on the effect on staff, partners and customers.
False: Models may not fully reflect reality, and no simulation result is perfectly accurate.
True: It is an organisational decision.
False: It is phase 3, after goals and simulation.
True: That gives a four-cell grid.

9.q: Which of the following statement(s) about functional and non-functional requirements is/are true?
o: A non-functional requirement states how the system should be.
Performance and security are non-functional.
Both kinds describe only user interactions.
A functional requirement states what the system should do.
Authentication behaviour is a non-functional requirement by definition.
w: True: It describes qualities and constraints such as speed or uptime.
True: They describe how well or how safely the system works, not what it does.
False: Non-functional requirements describe qualities such as performance, not interactions.
True: It describes behaviour, features and data handling.
False: Requiring users to authenticate describes what the system does, so it is functional; uptime is the non-functional kind.

9.q: Which of the following statement(s) about actors and use cases is/are true?
o: An actor must be a human.
An actor is a generic role, not a person's name.
A use case is a verb–noun phrase.
An association connects two actors.
A use case is drawn as a stick figure.
w: False: An actor can also be a device or an external system.
True: The model must work for every person who holds the role.
True: For example, Book Ticket.
False: It connects an actor and a use case with a solid line.
False: A use case is an oval; the stick figure is an actor.

9.q: Which of the following statement(s) about deriving use cases from a workflow is/are true?
o: An interactive activity becomes a use case for the human actor.
Automated use cases should be combined into one.
Manual activities become no use case.
Extra use cases are never needed.
An automated activity between two systems gives a client/server pair.
w: True: It is a candidate use case linked to the person who performs it.
False: They must not be combined, even when it seems logical.
True: They involve no system, so there is nothing for the system to do.
False: Authentication, search and CRUD-style view features may be needed beyond the workflow.
True: The sender has the use case as client and the receiver as server.

9.q: Which of the following statement(s) about use case packages is/are true?
o: Use cases of different systems must not share a package.
Integration use cases are typically grouped in an Integration package.
Two systems' integration use cases share one Integration package.
Login and Reset Password can form an Authentication package.
A package needs no name.
w: True: Packages are built within one system.
True: Each system keeps its own integration package.
False: Rule one forbids it, so each system has its own.
True: Related use cases are grouped and given a function name.
False: Each package gets a unique function name describing its overall functionality.

9.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the Function Model is/are true?
o: It records change type, system ownership and technical notes.
It replaces the Use Case Model.
It organises use cases by system and functional area.
A feature done by hand today but already supported by a system is Unchanged.
New means the system already supports the use case.
9.e: System, function, use case, change type, notes.
w: True: These are what it adds to the use cases.
False: It builds on the use cases by adding an implementation view.
True: That gives a view of ownership and grouping.
True: Change type describes the system, not the business practice.
False: New means the use case is not yet supported, for example because it is done manually today.

10.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the Concept Solution Blueprint is/are true?
o: It does not commit to technical implementation details at this stage.
It is the same document as the Detailed Solution Blueprint.
It gives an initial high-level view of the end-to-end solution.
Its framework has three steps: Architecture, Risk and Cost modelling.
It fixes the operating system and vendor.
w: True: Choices such as vendor or operating system come later.
False: The detailed blueprint further refines it in later work.
True: Detailed design follows later.
True: Each step produces a model.
False: It deliberately avoids specific implementation details.

10.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the C4 model is/are true?
o: A Component diagram is used only if it adds value.
The Code diagram is recommended for every team.
It has four diagram types: Context, Container, Component and Code.
A container is an application or data store.
Context and Container diagrams are recommended for most teams.
w: True: Most teams stop at the Container level.
False: It is rarely used and can be generated from existing code.
True: Each zooms into one box of the level above.
True: It is not Docker.
True: Component diagrams only when they add value.

10.q: Which of the following statement(s) about risk modelling is/are true?
o: Elimination means accepting the outcome of the event.
Reduction can lower either the probability or the impact of an adverse event.
Risk types include goal, process flow, data, technology and organisational.
Rating A is the highest rating.
Acceptance means shifting the risk to others.
w: False: Elimination avoids the activity that introduces the risk; accepting is Acceptance.
True: Defence lowers probability and mitigation lowers impact.
True: Five types are named.
True: It follows from high impact with medium or high likelihood, or medium impact with high likelihood.
False: Shifting risk is Transfer; Acceptance means doing nothing.

10.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the concept cost model is/are true?
o: It is qualitative.
It rates fixed cost, maintenance cost and total cost.
It is filled with dollar estimates.
Items such as software and deployment can be rated.
It is built before the architecture model.
w: True: Each item is rated Low, Med or High.
True: A justification column explains each rating.
False: That is a common mistake; dollars come later, when vendors and technology are fixed.
True: Each item and sub-item receives its own rating.
False: Architecture comes first, then risk, then cost.

11.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the Magic Triangle is/are true?
o: How? corresponds to the value chain.
Who? is at the centre.
It has five corners.
Value? corresponds to the value proposition.
What? corresponds to the value proposition.
w: True: The course ties it to process.
True: It asks who the target customer segment is.
False: It has one centre and three corners.
False: Value? is the revenue model; the value proposition is What?.
True: The course ties it to product.

11.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the three types of innovation is/are true?
o: Process innovation changes only How?.
Business model innovation changes only Value?.
Process innovation changes Who? only.
Business model innovation changes two or more corners.
Product innovation changes only What?.
w: True: It changes the value chain.
False: A single corner is not enough; two or more must change.
False: It changes How?; Who? is the customer segment.
True: For example the value proposition and the key activities.
True: It changes the product or service.

11.q: Which of the following statement(s) about creativity, invention and innovation is/are true?
o: Innovation is the commercialisation of an invention.
Innovation precedes invention.
Invention creates something new using scientific skills.
Innovation is usually restricted to R&D.
Creativity concerns novel, useful ideas.
w: True: It uses strategy, technical and marketing skills.
False: Invention precedes innovation.
True: It may never be commercialised.
False: That describes invention; innovation spreads across the organisation.
True: It is about thinking new things.

11.q: Which of the following statement(s) about process innovation is/are true?
o: Radical innovation is riskier than incremental improvement.
Incremental improvement affects a broader part of the organisation than radical innovation.
Radical innovation can increase value by 50%, 100% or more.
Process reengineering is a traditional term for incremental improvement.
Radical innovation needs less cultural change.
w: True: It requires more cultural and structural change.
False: Radical innovation affects a broader portion.
True: Incremental improvement generates limited value.
False: It is a traditional term for process innovation, not incremental improvement.
False: It needs a higher level of cultural and structural change.

12.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the automation spectrum is/are true?
o: Intelligent automation embeds AI in workflows.
Traditional digital automation works on structured data with explicit rules.
Agentic automation removes the human role entirely.
RPA interacts through the application user interface.
Agentic automation uses goals, policies and constraints.
w: True: It uses decision rules and predictive models on structured and unstructured data.
True: Its path is predefined.
False: A human approves, supervises or intervenes.
True: It uses explicit rules and a predefined path.
True: It selects its path dynamically within them.

12.q: Which of the following statement(s) about digital twins and IoT is/are true?
o: Control is the level where a human only observes data.
IoT devices sense or act on their environment.
An IoT device can be modelled as a technology participant with its own lane.
A digital twin is a static image of an asset.
A digital twin is updated using real-world data.
w: False: That is Monitor; Control changes the environment through a system or actuator.
True: They exchange data with digital systems.
True: It is treated like a system with automated activities.
False: It is a dynamic representation that is kept up to date.
True: Often through IoT sensors.

12.q: Which of the following statement(s) about IoT BPMN tasks is/are true?
o: A service task is a control system calling a device or service.
A user task is a human using a software application.
A timer start event ends the process.
A send task receives a message.
A script task is an IoT device's own hardware function.
w: True: It involves system-to-system communication.
True: It is an interactive activity.
False: It starts a process on a time-date or cycle.
False: A send task sends one to a participant in another pool.
True: It is executed by the process engine.

12.q: Which of the following statement(s) about IoT architecture and challenges is/are true?
o: Compatibility is a named challenge.
The application layer is the lowest layer.
Five challenges are named.
IoT business process management sits in the service support layer.
The smart device / sensor layer is the lowest layer.
w: True: It concerns non-unified cloud services, missing M2M standards and diverse firmware.
False: It is the top layer, holding smart environments such as cities and homes.
False: Four are named: security, privacy, connectivity and compatibility.
True: Business process modelling and execution are placed there.
True: Sensors and devices sit at the bottom of the stack.

13.q: Which of the following statement(s) about process types is/are true?
o: A sub-process is a type of management process.
A management process is also called a value chain.
A supporting process provides outputs that are inputs to core processes.
A core process produces what external customers receive.
A management process provides directions, rules and best practices.
w: False: It is a smaller process inside a core or supporting process.
False: The value chain is the core process.
True: It facilitates the operation of the core.
True: It embodies critical corporate expertise.
True: It plans, measures and controls.

13.q: Which of the following statement(s) about value chains is/are true?
o: Value is the cost of production.
The course shows two notations for drawing value chains.
Organisations typically support 3 to 15 value chains.
The generic value chain model has three primary activities.
A value chain includes the activities to design, produce, market, deliver and support a product.
w: False: Value is what buyers are willing to pay.
True: They are the Porter Value Chain Model and the SAP Business Map.
True: Studying them aligns investment with value creation.
False: It has five primary activities: inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, and service.
True: That is Porter's view.

13.q: Which of the following statement(s) about the Process Executive and Hierarchy models is/are true?
o: The Process Executive Model goes down to level 6.
A process bar spanning several columns means only one unit is involved.
The Process Executive Model shows functional units as columns.
The Process Hierarchy Model shows functional units as columns.
The Process Hierarchy Model starts from a level-3 process.
w: False: It stops at level 3 to manage complexity; deeper levels use hierarchy models.
False: It means all the spanned functional units are involved.
True: Processes are drawn across them.
False: It is a tree of processes and sub-processes.
True: It should not repeat the Process Executive Model.

13.q: Which of the following statement(s) about industry reference frameworks is/are true?
o: SCOR is for supply chain management.
The APQC Process Classification Framework is cross-industry.
eTOM is cross-industry.
SCOR is for telecoms.
eTOM is for telecoms.
w: True: It is the Supply Chain Operations Reference.
True: Unlike the industry-specific frameworks.
False: Cross-industry is the Process Classification Framework.
False: That is eTOM.
True: It is the Enhanced Telecom Operations Map.

14.q: Which of the following statement(s) about choosing the right process model is/are true?
o: Structure and reporting questions go to the Organisation Model.
Geography questions go to the Resource Model.
Sequence and interaction questions go to the Process Workflow Model.
Decision logic questions go to the Business Rules Model.
Who-and-what inventory questions go to the Business Rules Model.
w: True: Who reports to whom.
False: Geography is the Location Model.
True: It is by far the most common answer.
True: Rules explain the conditions.
False: Inventory is the Resource Model.

14.q: Which of the following statement(s) about choosing an analysis technique is/are true?
o: Questions about waiting or randomness need dynamic analysis.
A qualitative “why” question stays static.
Questions about alternatives or “how many” need dynamic analysis.
“Where does work queue up?” is answered by a static report.
“Which fix first?” is answered by the RCR model.
w: True: Static analysis cannot see queues.
True: RCI answers it.
True: What-if analysis tests alternatives and resource numbers.
False: It needs bottleneck analysis.
True: Impact and complexity rank the fixes.

14.q: Which of the following statement(s) about common mistakes is/are true?
o: Business rules attach to activities, not gateways.
Impact 5 means Very Low.
Complexity 5 means Very Complex.
The longest task is not automatically the bottleneck.
A static report does not show waiting.
w: True: The gateway only shows a branch.
False: Impact 5 is Very High.
False: Complexity 5 is Very Easy.
True: Queue and over-use matter too.
True: There are no queues in it.

14.q: Which of the following statement(s) about mapping activity types to artefacts is/are true?
o: Automated system-to-system activities give a client/server pair.
Interactive activities give one use case for the human actor.
Manual activities give no use case.
Automated activities sit in a human lane.
Interactive activities give no use case.
w: True: Or a send task and message event across pools.
True: They may map to user tasks in IoT notation.
True: They involve no system.
False: They sit in a system lane.
False: They give one.

lessons.title: Big Picture & Business Language
lessons.goal: See the Model → Analyse → Solve → Innovate journey and the four dimensions used to describe any business.
lessons.subtitle: See the Model → Analyse → Solve → Innovate journey and the four dimensions used to describe any business.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersEvery later model answers one of four questions about a business. Knowing the journey tells you which tool to reach for next.
🧠 Memory hookPurpose · Participants · Process · Product = Why · Who · How · What.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
1Big-Picture Overview→2Understanding "Business Language":…
⚡ At a glance — The four-chapter journey
Model→Analyse→Solve→Innovate
🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
NameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
ModelBuilds the As-Is models of what the business does today.First stage; nothing is judged yet.
AnalyseStudies the As-Is models for issues and recommendations, then models the To-Be.Judges the current state.
SolveTurns the To-Be into IT solution requirements and solutioning models.Specifies the system, not the business change.
InnovateFeeds technology-driven ideas into new To-Be designs.Last stage; looks beyond fixing existing processes.
Purpose (Why?)Mission, vision and strategic goals — the business's North Star.The reason the business exists.
Participants (Who?)Every stakeholder, team, customer, system and AI agent, internal and external.People and systems, not activities.
Process (How?)The value-chain operations and workflows that connect participants.The work itself.
Product (What?)What is delivered: physical or digital goods and services, or hybrids.The outcome the customer receives.
Not a member: “Project” is not a fourth P of business language. In the As-Is/To-Be comparison table the fourth row is labelled Project (the IT solution), which is a different use of the word.
1.1Big-Picture Overview

The course follows one story arc:

flowchart LR
    A["MODEL<br/>the Model chapter"] --> B["ANALYSE<br/>the Analyse chapter"] --> C["SOLVE<br/>the Solve chapter"] --> D["INNOVATE<br/>the Innovate chapter"]
    style A fill:#f28b82,color:#000
    style B fill:#8ab4f8,color:#000
    style C fill:#81c995,color:#000
    style D fill:#fdd663,color:#000

Read the arc as four chapters: Model, Analyse, Solve and Innovate. The "Big Picture" diagram below is the most repeated idea in the course:

flowchart LR
    subgraph PROBLEM["Problem Space"]
        direction TB
        NC["Need for Change"] --> AISM["AS-IS Process Modelling"]
        BN["Business Needs"] --> AISMO["AS-IS Models"]
        AISM --> AISMO
        AISMO --> AISA["AS-IS Process Analysis"]
        AISA --> IR["Issues & Recommendations"]
    end
    subgraph SOLUTION["Solution Space"]
        direction TB
        TBM["TO-BE Process Modelling"] --> TBMO["TO-BE Models"]
        TBMO --> TBA["TO-BE Process Analysis"]
        TBA --> SolM["Solutioning Models"]
        SolM --> ITR["IT Solution Requirements"]
    end
    IR --> TBM

Read this diagram left to right:

  • Model = build the As-Is Models (what we do today).
  • Analyse = study those As-Is models to find Issues & Recommendations, then model the To-Be (future) state.
  • Solve = turn To-Be models into concrete IT solution requirements (IT functional and non-functional requirements), expressed in the solutioning models: use case, function, architecture, risk and cost models.
  • Innovate = technology-driven ideas feed new To-Be designs. The three innovation types behind it are product, process and business model innovation; enterprise-level process architecture completes the chapter.
1.2Understanding "Business Language": The Four Dimensions

Before you can model anything, you need a shared vocabulary for describing a business. The course frames every business along four dimensions:

Dimension Question Definition Example
Purpose Why? Mission, vision, strategic goals — the business's "North Star" "Lead claims processing for auto insurance"
Participants Who? Every stakeholder, team, customer, system, and now AI agent, internal and external Sales agent, Store Keeper, AI chatbot
Process How? The value-chain operations and workflows that connect participants to deliver value The order-fulfilment workflow
Product What? What is actually delivered to the customer: physical goods, digital goods, physical services, digital services, or hybrids A sandwich, an insurance policy, a mobile app

Why this matters: almost every model you'll build in this course is really just a detailed answer to one of these four questions, applied to one specific process. Keep this table in your head.

Purpose = "Why / Value" and the North Star. Purpose is the reason a business exists: to create value. You unite the whole organisation by finding a single North Star Metric that measures that value. The course name the idea but give no worked metric, so treat it as vocabulary: the dimension the later performance goals are traced back to.

✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • The course runs Model → Analyse → Solve → Innovate.
  • Model builds As-Is models; Analyse finds issues and designs the To-Be.
  • Solve turns the To-Be into IT solution requirements.
  • Innovate feeds technology and business-model ideas into the To-Be.
  • Every business is described by Purpose, Participants, Process and Product.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Four dimensions of a businesstap to flip
Purpose (Why), Participants (Who), Process (How), Product (What).
What does Analyse produce?tap to flip
Issues and recommendations from the As-Is, then the To-Be model.
North Star Metrictap to flip
A single metric that measures the value a business creates.
Participants include…tap to flip
People, teams, customers, systems and AI agents, inside and outside the business.
➡ Where next? Next you learn how IT and business strategy line up, and how the BPM cycle keeps processes improving.

lessons.title: Business–IT Alignment & BPM
lessons.goal: Explain why IT must follow business goals and how the BPM cycle keeps processes improving.
lessons.subtitle: Explain why IT must follow business goals and how the BPM cycle keeps processes improving.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersMisaligned IT wastes money and slows the business. BPM is the ongoing effort that keeps aligning and improving processes.
🧠 Memory hookDiscover → Model & Analyse → Design Solution → Implement Solution → Monitor & Optimise, then loop.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
1Business & IT Alignment→2Business Process Management
⚡ At a glance — BPM implementation cycle
Discover→Model & Analyse→Design Solution→Implement Solution→Monitor & Optimise
🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
NameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
Enterprise AlignmentAligns objectives, processes, information, applications and technology across the whole organisation.Whole-organisation scope; delivered via Enterprise Architecture.
Project AlignmentAligns the same list for one specific IT solution.One solution; delivered via the Business Process Engineering Methodology.
DiscoverUnderstands the current state; sets context and scope.Deliberately shallow; not the detailed model-building.
Model & AnalyseBuilds and studies the models to find issues and recommendations.Covers the Model and Analyse chapters.
Design SolutionDesigns the solution; corresponds to Solve.Specifies requirements and blueprint.
Implement SolutionBuilds and rolls out the solution.Delivery, covered in a later course.
Monitor & OptimiseMeasures and improves the running process; feeds back into the cycle.Why the cycle never ends.
Mission, vision and business objectives sit above strategies in the strategy cascade; objectives are the measurable, time-bound level.
2.1Business & IT Alignment

The core question: are business goals actually driving technology decisions, and do IT capabilities enable business innovation? The course frames misalignment as a symptom of five specific failures — memorize these as diagnostic questions, not vague platitudes:

Alignment Question What goes wrong without it
Are business goals driving technology decisions? Wasted IT investment, missed opportunities
Do IT capabilities enable business innovation? IT becomes a bottleneck, not an enabler
Is there shared accountability for outcomes? Siloed thinking, finger-pointing on failed projects
Are communication channels effective between teams? Requirements gaps, unrealistic expectations
Is technology strategy integrated with business strategy? Conflicting priorities, duplicated effort

Root causes of misalignment:

  1. Lack of appreciation of business processes by IT.
  2. Lack of appreciation of IT value by the business.
  3. Lack of a common language between IT and business.
  4. Growing business and a changing environment (alignment isn't a one-time fix).

Steps toward alignment:

  1. Recognise IT as a transformative tool, not just a cost centre.
  2. Use IT to target customers both internally and externally.
  3. Get IT and business staff to "talk to each other" in mutually comprehensible language.
  4. Define clear, coherent goals/objectives for the IT department.
  5. Demand reliable, measurable ROI from IT systems.
  6. Write it all down: one document enumerating both IT and business strategy.

"IT doesn't matter" debate (Nicholas Carr): Carr argued IT is becoming a commodity, not a source of competitive advantage. The course's counter-argument: differentiation doesn't come from owning IT, it comes from how IT is combined with strategy, processes, and organisational capability. Without Business-IT alignment, IT genuinely does become a commodity — alignment is what creates the differentiation. (And now, extend "IT" to include AI agents.)

Levels of Alignment

The course distinguishes two scopes of alignment, and one deliverable methodology for each:

Level Scope Aligns Delivered via
Enterprise Alignment Whole organisation Business objectives, processes, information, applications, technology — across the entire org Enterprise Architecture
Project Alignment One IT solution The same list, but in the context of delivering one specific solution Business Process Engineering Methodology 
flowchart TB
    E["Enterprise Alignment<br/>(Enterprise Architecture)"]
    P["Project Alignment<br/>(Business Process Engineering Methodology)"]
    Pr["Process"]
    T["Technology: Blueprinting, Implementation & Operations"]
    E --> P
    E --> T
    P --> Pr --> T

Practical framing — "Voice of the Business" (As-Is vs To-Be): this table is how the four dimensions from get reused later once you start comparing current vs. future state (this becomes central in Analyse):

Category Question As-Is To-Be
Purpose Why? As-Is Mission/Vision/Business Goals To-Be Mission/Vision/Business Goals
Participants Who? As-Is Business Participants (human or systems) To-Be Business Participants
Process How? As-Is Business Process To-Be Business Process
Project What? Current IT Solution Proposed IT Solution
2.2Business Process Management

Definition (BABOK® Guide v3, IIBA): BPM is a management discipline and set of enabling technologies that:

  • focuses on how the organisation performs work to deliver value across multiple functional areas to customers/stakeholders,
  • aims for a view of value delivery that spans the entire organisation, and
  • views the organisation through a process-centric lens.

A BPM initiative delivers value by improving how work is performed. It governs how manual and automated processes are created, modified, cancelled, and governed. Process-centric organisations treat BPM as an ongoing effort, not a one-off project.

The strategy cascade (how a mission becomes a running process improvement cycle):

flowchart TD
    MV["Mission & Vision<br/><i>e.g. Lead claims processing for auto insurance</i>"] --> BO["Business Objectives<br/><i>e.g. Cut auto claims fraud 80% in 2 years</i>"]
    BO --> ST["Strategies to Achieve the Goals<br/><i>High-level plans / resource allocation, e.g. expand into new markets</i>"]
    ST --> IP["Implementation Phases<br/>(the BPM cycle — see below)"]

Examples given for each level of the cascade:

Level Examples (auto-insurance company)
Mission and Vision "Accelerate growth in the auto insurance business"; "Lead claims processing for auto insurance business"; "Provide affordable and reliable auto insurance services"
Business Objectives "Achieve 30% increase in revenue in the auto insurance business"; "Support on-line auto insurance claims processing by the end of the fiscal year"; "Cut auto claims fraud by 80% within the next two years"
Strategies to achieve the goals High-level plans or approaches designed to achieve business goals and objectives; they guide resource allocation and decision-making. Example: "Expand into new geographic markets and launch a targeted marketing campaign to increase brand awareness."

The pattern to notice: a mission/vision is directional and qualitative; an objective is measurable and time-bound (30%, 80%, "two years", "end of the fiscal year"). That measurability is what later lets a process performance goal be tested by simulation.

Mission vs vision. Both are foundational, concise, memorable statements that align employees, stakeholders and customers around the organisation's purpose, and they usually work together. They differ as follows:

Mission statement Vision statement
Time focus Present and near future — what the company does now Future — where the company aspires to be
Purpose Current purpose, objectives and approach Desired future state and long-term aspirations
Scope Concrete and specific: what it does and whom it serves Abstract and broad: the overall impact it hopes to have
Actionability Guides day-to-day operations and decisions Inspirational; a long-term goal to strive towards
Audience Internal and external (employees, customers, stakeholders) Mainly employees and relevant stakeholders

Strategy vs goal: strategies are broad statements from high-level management; goals are measurable, often with a time span; you then figure out how to achieve the goals. The notes add that a business strategy weighs three elements — the company, its customers and the competition — and answers which markets and geographies to engage, which products and services to provide, the nature of competition, the major competitive differentiators, and how well the organisation can adapt to changing customer needs.

Implementation Phases — the BPM cycle. This is the operational engine that keeps turning as long as the organisation exists:

flowchart TD
    Discover(["Discover"]) --> ModelAnalyse(["Model & Analyse"])
    ModelAnalyse --> DesignSolution(["Design Solution"])
    DesignSolution --> ImplementSolution(["Implement Solution"])
    ImplementSolution --> MonitorOptimize(["Monitor & Optimize"])
    MonitorOptimize --> Discover

Each named phase of this course maps onto that cycle:

BPM Cycle Phase Course Chapter
Discover (start of) Model
Model & Analyse Model + Analyse
Design Solution Solve
Implement Solution Process Solution Implementation
Monitor & Optimise Optimisation → BPAS; Monitoring and Change Management → covered in a later course

Inside "Model & Analyse" — the two-stage structure of the Model and Analyse chapters:

the problem-space / solution-space steps that the whole Model + Analyse phase walks through.

flowchart LR
    subgraph PS["Define Problem Space"]
        direction TB
        A1["1. Select Process"] --> A2["2. Model AS-IS"] --> A3["3. Analyse AS-IS"] --> A4["4. Approve AS-IS"]
    end
    subgraph SS["Define Solution Space"]
        direction TB
        B1["1. Model TO-BE"] --> B2["2. Analyse TO-BE"] --> B3["3. Approve TO-BE"] --> B4["4. Create IT Solution"]
    end
    PS --> SS

The Discover Phase in detail

What is Discovery? Understanding the current state: "What are we actually doing now?" Objectives:

  • Identify current processes and gather stakeholder requirements (process owners, end users, customers, SMEs).
  • Assess current performance: baseline metrics/KPIs, bottlenecks, inefficiencies.
  • Document process content; identify system dependencies/integrations; understand compliance requirements.

Discovery is deliberately shallow — it sets context. The detailed elicitation (the actual model-building covered in below) is a separate, deeper step that follows it.

Deliverables of Discovery:

Expected Outputs Challenges Mitigation
Complete list of in-scope processes Limited stakeholder availability Schedule in advance; offer flexible timing
Stakeholder roles and responsibilities Incomplete/outdated documentation Observe and interview instead of trusting docs
Current-state documentation Complex technical integration Engage IT early; document system interactions
Requirements specification
Baseline assessment

Elicitation technique — the Interview, structured around three buckets of questions:

flowchart LR
    People["People<br/>Identify the business users"] --> Goals["Goals<br/>Identify process goals & KPIs"] --> Process["Process<br/>Identify the steps, pain points, characteristics"]

Also gather: location information and organisational structure (People bucket).

✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • Alignment asks whether business goals drive technology decisions.
  • Misalignment comes from poor mutual appreciation, no common language and a changing environment.
  • Enterprise alignment is whole-organisation; project alignment is one solution.
  • The BPM cycle repeats: Discover, Model & Analyse, Design Solution, Implement Solution, Monitor & Optimise.
  • Objectives are measurable and time-bound; missions and visions are directional.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Enterprise vs project alignmenttap to flip
Whole organisation via Enterprise Architecture vs one solution via the Business Process Engineering Methodology.
Mission vs visiontap to flip
Mission: what the company does now. Vision: where it aspires to be.
Why is Discovery shallow?tap to flip
It sets context and scope; deeper elicitation follows it.
Strategy vs goaltap to flip
Strategies are broad approaches; goals are measurable, often time-bound.
➡ Where next? Next: what exactly counts as a business process, and which questions describe one.

lessons.title: What Is a Business Process?
lessons.goal: Define a business process, name its components and use the six questions and three lenses to describe one.
lessons.subtitle: Define a business process, name its components and use the six questions and three lenses to describe one.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersYou cannot improve what you cannot describe. A shared definition lets analysts and the business talk about the same thing.
🧠 Memory hookRepeatable series of activities performed to deliver a service or product to a stakeholder.
⚡ At a glance — Describe any business with six questions
What?→How?→Why?→When?→Who?→Where?
🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
NameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
Business process (course definition)A repeatable series of activities performed to deliver a service or a product to a stakeholder.Repeatable and stakeholder-facing.
ProcessTransforms inputs into outputs using resources; started by business events.The whole: inputs to outputs, started by an event.
Sub-processA process at a smaller scale; decomposable into further activities.Marked with a + in BPMN.
ActivityA single logical step; the atomic unit for modelling.Not decomposed further.
Resources – Who?People and systems that perform the work.Lens: who or what.
Workflow – How?The ordered steps.Lens: the sequence.
Data – What?What goes in and comes out.Lens: inputs and outputs.
Business rules answer When?, not Why?. Why? is business strategy, objectives and KPIs.
3.1What Is a Business Process?

Three definitions were given, each adding something the previous one lacked:

Author/Year Definition What it added / what it's missing
Pall (1987) "The logical organisation of people, materials, energy, equipment, and procedures into work activities designed to produce a specified end result (work product)" ✅ Introduces the dimensions (people, materials, etc.) ❌ No explicit mention of IT/services
Feiler & Humphrey (1993) "A set of partially ordered steps intended to reach a goal" Simple and general, but very abstract
Course definition "A repeatable series of activities performed to deliver a service or a product to a stakeholder" The working definition used throughout BPAS

Unpacking the course definition — a business process:

  • consists of activities, each a set of logical steps performed by humans or systems;
  • transforms inputs into outputs according to guidance, using resources;
  • is initiated by one or more business events;
  • has performance indicators (KPIs) with measurable, evaluable objectives;
  • can be described along: How – Who – What – When – Where – Why.

Process vs. Sub-process vs. Activity:

Process = Sub-Processes + Activities
  • A sub-process is itself decomposable into further activities/sub-processes (it's a process at a smaller scale).
  • An activity is the atomic unit — a single logical step, not further decomposed for modelling purposes.

Key components of a business process

Key components of a business process:

  • a set of logical activities (tasks/steps) performed by human or machine;
  • initiated by one or more business events;
  • involves business documents (e.g., shipping notice, invoice);
  • involves resources: humans and systems (applications);
  • has a defined set of key performance indicators (KPIs);
  • may be further divided into sub-processes and activities.

Each item is checkable against the airport diagram: the arrival at the counter is the event; Booking Confirmation, Passport, Boarding Pass and Luggage Tag are the business documents (work products); Traveler/Staff/System are the resources; the "+" on "Process booking details" marks a sub-process.

The six questions about a business

Asked of any business (for example, a fast-food chain), the six questions reveal:

Question What it covers Where it appears in the course
What? Raw materials, data, input/output, products Work products and data
How? Workflow, process flow, enterprise processes Process Workflow Model
Why? Business strategy, business objectives, KPIs Purpose; KPIs feed performance goals
When? Time, business rules, business events Business events on the workflow; Business Rules Model
Who? People and systems involved — organisation structure, organisational units, roles, people; IT infrastructure, systems, applications Organisation Model + Resource Model
Where? Location information; online, face-to-face; dine-in, takeaway, delivery Location Model

Business rules sit under When?, not Why?.

Three lenses of a process model

Lens Label What it covers
People & systems Resources – Who? Who/what performs the work
Instructions Workflow – How? The ordered steps
Input/output Data – What? What goes in and comes out

Business Process Models — why bother?

  • Provide a focus for discussing operational-improvement opportunities.
  • Provide a common framework/language for stakeholders who don't naturally speak the same vocabulary (recall 's "lack of common language" as a root cause of misalignment).
  • Are a systematic approach to represent related information (as opposed to ad-hoc prose descriptions).

Caution: Modelling is resource intensive. Building all 5 models properly (below) is not free — it costs stakeholder time, analyst time, and tool licences. Part of your job as an analyst is choosing which models are actually needed for a given process, not modelling everything by default.

⚡ Quick examples
Activity or sub-process?
PointAn activity is atomic; a sub-process can be broken down further.
ExampleA step marked with a + in BPMN hides its own sub-workflow.
ExplanationThe + marker means the step is a sub-process, so it is decomposable.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • A business process is a repeatable series of activities delivering a service or product to a stakeholder.
  • It is started by business events and measured by KPIs.
  • A sub-process can be broken down further; an activity cannot.
  • The six questions: What, How, Why, When, Who, Where.
  • Modelling is resource-intensive, so choose only the models you need.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Course definition of a business processtap to flip
A repeatable series of activities performed to deliver a service or a product to a stakeholder.
Activity vs sub-processtap to flip
An activity is atomic; a sub-process decomposes into further activities.
Where do business rules sit among the six questions?tap to flip
Under When?, together with time and business events.
Three lenses of a process modeltap to flip
Resources (Who), Workflow (How), Data (What).
➡ Where next? Next: the models that capture a process, starting with people, places and resources.

lessons.title: Organisation, Location & Resource Models
lessons.goal: Use the first three process models to capture people, places and resources.
lessons.subtitle: Use the first three process models to capture people, places and resources.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersBefore drawing the workflow you must know who is involved, where they are and what they use.
🧠 Memory hookOrg = who reports to whom · Location = where · Resource = what is used, and who controls it.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
1The Five Business Process Models→2Overview→3Organisation Model→4Location Model→5Resource Model
⚡ At a glance — Choose by question
Roles and reporting → Organisation→Geography → Location→Humans and systems → Resource
🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
NameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
Organisation ModelRoles and reporting structures; informally “People Politics”.Who reports to whom.
Location ModelGeographic distribution of stakeholders.Where people are.
Resource ModelHumans and technologies, categorised internal vs external.Who or what is used, and do you control it.
Collaboration ModelThe fourth of the seven views (not one of the five studied).Named only; not modelled in depth.
Process Package ModelOne of the seven views.Named only.
Process Workflow ModelSequence of activities in BPMN.Covered in the next chapter.
Business Rules ModelRules applied when performing an activity.Covered in the next chapter.
Functional RoleAn organisational title, e.g. Salesclerk.Appears on the org chart.
Process RoleA role that exists because a process needs it, e.g. Requester.May not appear on the org chart.
Seven views in total: Organisation, Location, Resource, Collaboration, Process Package, Process Workflow and Business Rules. Five are studied. Collaboration and Process Package are the two not studied.
4.1The Five (of Seven) Business Process Models

A business process can be captured through 7 different "views" (each view = one model): Organisation, Location, Resource, Collaboration, Process Package, Process Workflow, and Business Rules. Rule of thumb: "you don't need to utilise all seven models — decide which model is most helpful in telling your story."

4.2Overview
Model Captures Key Question It Answers
Organisation Model Roles and reporting structures Who reports to whom? What's the org chart?
Location Model Geographic distribution of stakeholders Where is everyone physically located?
Resource Model Humans and systems involved, categorised internal/external Who/what is involved, and do we control it?
Process Workflow Model Sequence of activities and the process flow (BPMN) What happens, in what order, and who does it?
Business Rules Model The rules applied when performing an activity What logic/policy governs a decision or task?
4.3Organisation Model

Purpose: represents the relationship between stakeholders in the current organisational context — informally known as "People Politics". It helps you:

  • identify which stakeholder can supply what information;
  • determine access control for an eventual IT solution;
  • understand who the possible end-users are;
  • anticipate the impact on org structure if a process changes.

Building blocks:

  • Organisation — a legal entity that performs a business.
  • Department — a unit of an organisation tied to related functions.
  • Role — a logical grouping of a person's responsibilities. Two sub-types:
  • Functional Role — an organisational title, e.g. "Salesclerk".
  • Process Role — a role that exists because a process needs it, e.g. "Requester" in a Purchase Requisition process (this role may not appear anywhere on the org chart).

Worked example — catalogue retailer:

flowchart TD
    Org["Retail Company (Organisation)"] --> Sales["Sales (Department)"]
    Org --> Warehouse["Warehouse (Department)"]
    Sales --> RM["Regional Manager (Role)"]
    Sales --> SalesM["Sales Manager (Role)"]
    SalesM --> SA["Sales Agent (Role)"]
    Warehouse --> StoreM["Store Manager (Role)"]
    StoreM --> SK["Store Keeper (Role)"]

Worked example — Expense Report scenario:

flowchart TD
    CEO["CEO"] --> Managers["Managers (Group Role)"]
    CEO --> FinOfficer["Financial Officer (Individual Role)"]
    CEO --> OfficeAdmin["Office Administrator (Individual Role)"]
    Managers --> Employees["Employees (Group Role)"]

Note the distinction between Individual Role (one specific position, e.g. CEO, Financial Officer) and Group Role (a role held by many people, e.g. "Managers", "Employees").

4.4Location Model

Purpose: shows how stakeholders are distributed across physical locations. Helps with:

  • identifying location-specific needs (e.g. language);
  • input to IT solution deployment decisions;
  • understanding organisational relationships/coordination across sites;
  • awareness of different government policies per location;
  • cost implications of a distributed deployment;
  • level of technology/infrastructure available (internet access vs. leased line);
  • a very concrete gotcha: transactions spanning multiple time zones must use GMT;
  • local culture considerations.

Worked example — catalogue retailer, geographic hierarchy (Region → Subregion → Office → Department):

flowchart TD
    Org["Retail Company (Organisation)"] --> East["US East (Region)"]
    Org --> West["US West (Region)"]
    East --> NY["New York Office"]
    East --> Atlanta["Atlanta Office"]
    West --> Dallas["Dallas Office"]
    NY --> Sales1["Sales (Department)"]
    NY --> Warehouse1["Warehouse (Department)"]

Cross-reference: Organisation Model shows the reporting structure; Location Model shows the geographic structure. The same departments/roles can appear in both — they're two different "views" (cuts) of the same underlying stakeholder set. This is exactly why the course calls them separate models: one dataset, multiple diagrams, each answering a different elicitation question.

4.5Resource Model

Purpose: captures the humans and technologies involved in a process, categorised along two axes: internal vs. external, and (implicitly) human vs. technology. Visually the course draws this as a "bowl"/iceberg shape — everything above the waterline is external, below is internal; left of centre is human, right is technology.

Worked example — SUBWAY Sandwich Sales Process:

Internal External
Human Bread Artist, Veggie Artist, Cashier Customer
Technology Billing System —

Worked example — StarMall Rental Application Process:

Internal External
Human CSO (Customer Service Officer), OD (Office Dispatcher), MO (Marketing Officer), LM (Leasing Manager) Customers
Technology IMS (Industrial space Management System) Government UEN website

Worked example — Expense Report Process:

Internal External
Human Employee, Manager, Office Administrator, Financial Officer —
Technology — Workday Cloud System, Bank System

A resource only belongs in the model if it participates in the process — a system the company owns but which this specific process never touches doesn't belong here. Notice Workday Cloud System is classed external even though the company pays for it: internal/external in this model tracks who controls/operates the resource, not who uses it.

"You manage" : the light-blue bowl in the resource-model diagram is labelled You manage, and the vertical axis is labelled Resource Type. That is the mnemonic for internal vs external: internal = the resources you manage; external = the ones you do not, however much you depend on them.

✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • A process can be captured in seven views; choose the ones that tell your story.
  • The Organisation Model shows roles and reporting lines.
  • Functional roles appear on the org chart; process roles exist only because of a process.
  • The Location Model shows where stakeholders are; transactions across time zones use GMT.
  • The Resource Model sorts resources into internal/external and human/technology; internal means you manage it.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Functional vs process roletap to flip
Functional: an organisational title. Process: exists because the process needs it.
Internal vs external resourcetap to flip
Internal resources are the ones you manage; external ones you do not, however much you depend on them.
Which time standard is used for transactions across time zones?tap to flip
GMT.
Which two of the seven models are not studied?tap to flip
Collaboration and Process Package.
➡ Where next? Next: the workflow model in BPMN, and the business rules that sit behind its activities.

lessons.title: Workflow (BPMN) & Business Rules
lessons.goal: Read and draw BPMN workflows, classify activities and write business rules that attach to activities.
lessons.subtitle: Read and draw BPMN workflows, classify activities and write business rules that attach to activities.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersThe workflow is the heart of process modelling, and rules explain the IF/THEN logic the diagram cannot show.
🧠 Memory hookThe lane follows who performs the activity, not which tool is touched. Rules attach to activities, not gateways.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
1Process Workflow Model→2Business Rules Model
⚡ At a glance — Activity types
Manual→Interactive→Automated
🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
NameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
ManualPerformed by human effort, unaided by systems.Human lane; no system involved.
InteractiveDone by a human using a system.Still the human's lane, not the system's.
AutomatedDone entirely by a system.System lane; no human involvement.
Business EventStart or end that triggers or concludes the process (circle).Drawn as a circle; starts or ends the process.
Decision Point (gateway)Process branches on a condition (diamond).One flow in, several labelled flows out.
MergeSeveral incoming paths converge into one.Several flows in, one out; not a decision.
Parallel ActivitiesBranches run simultaneously (diamond with plus).AND, not exclusive.
SwimlaneGroups the activities of one Business Participant.A horizontal band named after the performer.
TransitionSequence flow between elements.A solid arrow between elements.
Work product / AssociationDocument or data object linked to an activity.A dashed arrow to a document or data object.
TimerA waiting period that can drive a loop.A clock icon; a wait that can drive a loop.
Rule-set template fields, in order: Name · Activity Using this Rule Set · Description · Rule Set · Related Rule Set. Annotations on a reviewed diagram: process trigger, association, usage of systems, execution time, probability.
5.1Process Workflow Model

This is the model most people think of when they hear "business process diagram" — the flowchart-with-swimlanes.

Business Participant — who can appear in a workflow:

  • Roles (supervisor, manager),
  • Departments (finance, sales),
  • Systems (service-centre system, order-entry system, AI Chatbot).

A participant is only given a swimlane if they actually perform an activity in this specific process — being a stakeholder isn't enough.

Activity types — the automation spectrum (this taxonomy is tested and reused constantly):

Type Definition Example Swimlane placement
Manual Performed by human effort, unaided by systems "Pack Goods" The human/role's lane
Interactive Done by a human using a system "Enter Order" The human/role's lane (not the system's!)
Automated Done entirely by a system, no human involvement "Retrieve Orders" The system's lane

Common mistake: putting an interactive activity in the system's swimlane because "a system is involved." The rule is about who performs the activity, not what tools they touch — a human entering data into a system is still the human's action, so it stays in the human's lane.

Why the three types matter later: in Solve the activity type decides whether an activity becomes a use case at all — manual → none, interactive → one use case for the human actor, automated between two systems → a client/server pair. The same split reappears in Innovate as BPMN user, script and service tasks for IoT.

BPMN Notation Legend

Use this legend to read any diagram in the course:

Symbol Meaning
⭕ (circle) Business Event — a start or end event that triggers/concludes the process
◇ (diamond) Decision Point (a.k.a. gateway) — the process branches based on a condition
▭ (rounded rectangle) Activity — a task performed by a participant
Horizontal band Swimlane — groups all activities performed by one Business Participant
Solid arrow Transition — sequence flow from one element to the next
Dashed/dotted arrow Work product / Association — a document or data object linked to an activity (e.g. "Sales Order", "Passport")
⬡ (small diamond, unlabelled) Merge — multiple incoming paths converge back into one
⭕ with arrow looping back Loop — an activity or sequence repeats
➕ (diamond with plus) Parallel Activities (AND-split/join) — branches execute simultaneously, not exclusively
Small clock icon on a flow ("Wait for a day") Timer — a waiting period that drives a loop (used in the Order Management example)
Vertical label at the left of a band Business Participant — the owner of that swimlane
✖ inside a diamond Exclusive-gateway marker. In the course both a decision point (one flow in, several labelled flows out) and a merge (several flows in, one out) are drawn this way, so tell them apart by counting flows, not by the shape

A Flow Diagram (as opposed to formal BPMN) is explicitly called out as "a broad, non-standardised term referring to any diagram that visually represents flow through a system" — i.e., simpler box-and-arrow charts without lanes are a looser, non-standard notation, still useful for quick communication but not equivalent to a proper BPMN swimlane diagram.

Reading an annotated real-world diagram (from the StarMall Signavio screenshot)

When you open an actual modelling tool (Signavio/Camunda/bpmn.io) on a finished diagram, these are the elements analysts specifically call out when reviewing it:

  • Process trigger — the start event (what kicks the process off, e.g. "Customer walk-in").
  • Association — the dotted line connecting an activity to a work product/document/system it uses.
  • Usage of systems — the small computer icon attached to a lane/activity showing which IT system is used.
  • Execution time — a number annotated on/near an activity indicating how long it takes (this feeds directly into Analyse's simulation/timing work).
  • Probability — a percentage on a gateway's outgoing paths (e.g. "75% eligible / 25% not eligible") showing how often each branch is taken — also feeds forward into process simulation later in the course.
5.2Business Rules Model

Purpose: captures the business rules applicable to activities in the Process Workflow Model.

  • Expressed in plain English (or another natural language) — not pseudocode, not a formal grammar.
  • Heavy use of business domain vocabulary.
  • Both manual and automated activities may require documented business rules.

Structure: IF <condition(s)> THEN <consequence>, chained with AND/OR, sometimes with an ELSE.

Worked examples:

IF a customer has a gold account
THEN discount is 20%

IF a customer has a gold account
THEN issue a gold credit card
ELSE issue a standard credit card

IF total miles earned is > 10,000
THEN change status from blue to silver

IF loan type is first mortgage
THEN occupancy status must be principal residence

IF borrower is student
THEN maximum number of books allowed is 10

IF travel is to overseas destination
THEN approval from Project Manager is required

The course's second column is an insurance-claim rule set:

If Claimant is an employee
AND injury occurred on premise
AND there is medical necessity
AND procedure is covered
THEN adjust amount billed

If Claimant is an employee
AND injury occurred off-premise
THEN reject claim

If Claimant is not an employee
THEN reject claim

Common mistake: Students often assume business rules attach to decision gateways (the diamonds). Business rules are used in activities, not decision gateways. The gateway just shows that a branch exists; the rule governing how that branch is decided lives with the activity that evaluates it (e.g. a "Determine Credit Worthiness" activity, not the diamond after it).

A rule set as a document — "Deciding Credit Worthiness"
