lessons.title: Choosing Models, Techniques & Artefacts
lessons.goal: Pick the right model, analysis technique or artefact for a question, and avoid the common mistakes.
lessons.subtitle: Pick the right model, analysis technique or artefact for a question, and avoid the common mistakes.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersExam-style questions give you a question and ask which tool answers it first. This chapter is the map.
🧠 Memory hookStructure → Organisation · Inventory → Resource · Flow → Workflow · Logic → Rules · Geography → Location.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
1Choosing the Right Model —…→2Choosing the Right Analysis Technique→3Choosing the Right Solve / Innovate…→4Common Mistakes & Gotchas
⚡ At a glance — Question → model
Organisation→Resource→Workflow→Business Rules→Location
14.1Choosing the Right Model — Elicitation Question Map

A recurring exam-style activity: given an elicitation question, which model answers it first? Consolidated:

Elicitation Question Best Model
Which roles are working in the department? Organisation
What is the structure of the teams? Who is the boss? Organisation
Which are the systems and roles within the process scope? Resource
Who are the customers and suppliers? Resource
Who are the participants in this activity? Workflow
Which departments does your department interact with? Workflow
What happens next? / How does the process start? Workflow
What is the system-to-system interaction within the process scope? Workflow
What do the systems send to the roles in the organisation? Workflow
What happens when you reject a customer's request? Workflow
Do customers interact with systems or roles? Workflow
On average, how many rejections do you handle per day? Workflow (feeds into later process analysis/simulation)
How do you check if a request is a fraud case? Business Rules
How do you decide on the discount amount for a customer? Business Rules
Where are your customers'/departments' offices located? Location

Pattern to memorise: structure & reporting → Organisation; inventory of who/what is involved → Resource; sequence, flow, and interaction → Workflow (by far the most common answer); decision logic → Business Rules; geography → Location.

14.2Choosing the Right Analysis Technique
flowchart TD
    Q["What do you need to find out?"] --> A{"Do you need numbers from running the process?"}
    A -->|"No: why does the problem exist?"| RC["Static: RCI model, then RCR model"]
    A -->|"Basic time, cost, workload from known task times"| SR["Static report"]
    A -->|Yes| B{"Does the process exist today?"}
    B -->|"Yes: find bottlenecks, set a baseline"| AS["Dynamic: simulate As-Is (or pilot test)"]
    B -->|"No: compare redesigns"| TB["Dynamic: simulate To-Be scenarios, what-if"]
    TB --> IM["Then: impact analysis and final selection"]

Read it top-down: qualitative why questions and quick arithmetic stay static; anything involving waiting, randomness, alternatives or "how many resources" requires dynamic analysis. Simulation results are never the last step — impact analysis and management decisions still gate the final choice.

Question Technique
Why does this issue exist, and what is the common cause of several issues? RCI model (5-Why / fishbone)
Which fix should we do first? RCR model (impact score × complexity)
What is the cycle time / cost per instance; is a role over-used? Static report
Where does work queue up? Bottleneck analysis (queue + utilisation + activity times)
Which paths cost most / get rejected? Path analysis (expected contribution = share × value)
How many servers/staff do we need to hit a goal? What-if analysis
What if a rare disaster happens? Unusual event analysis
Who else is affected by this To-Be? Impact analysis (internal/external, hard/soft)

Which kind of simulation data is it?

If the item is… It is… Example
How often / when the process is triggered, opening hours Process-wide 6,500 requests a year; Mon–Fri 9:00–17:00
How long one task takes, or what it costs, or which resource it needs Activity-related 5 min mean, s.d. 45 s
Who does the work: cost per hour, headcount, working hours Resource-related 3 Sales Agents at $50/h
The chance a gateway sends work down a branch Decision points 70% Yes / 30% No; resubmission rate
Detail that changes none of the above Not applicable Patient name and age
14.3Choosing the Right Solve / Innovate Artefact
Question Artefact
What must the system do for each user? Use Case Model (actors, use cases, associations)
Is this requirement about behaviour or about quality (speed, uptime, security)? Functional vs non-functional classification
Which use cases belong together and what is each group called? Use Case Packages
Which system builds each feature, and is it new, modified or unchanged? Function Model
What is in scope, who uses it, and which outside systems does it talk to? C4 Context diagram
What deployable applications and data stores make up the system? C4 Container diagram
How is one application organised internally? C4 Component diagram
What could go wrong, how bad, and what do we do about it? Risk Model + rating matrix
Roughly how expensive is each part? Concept Cost Model (Low/Med/High)
How much should a step be automated, and who stays in the loop? Automation spectrum
How do I draw sensors and devices in BPMN? IoT lanes/pools, script/service/send tasks, message and timer events
Which kind of innovation is this? Gassmann Magic Triangle + old/new table; count the corners that change
What does the whole business model look like? Business Model Canvas (nine blocks → four triangle corners)
What are all the organisation's processes, and who runs them? Process Executive Model (functional units × processes, 2–3 levels)
What is inside one level-3 process? Process Hierarchy Model (L3 → L4 → L5 …)
Is this process core, support or management? Process type definitions

Activity type → use case → BPMN-IoT task, in one table:

Activity type Use case IoT advanced notation
Manual None — (plain task, no marker)
Interactive One, linked to the human actor User task
Automated, one system One per action Script task (device's own function)
Automated, system-to-system A client/server pair Service task, or send task + message event across pools
14.4Common Mistakes & Gotchas
  1. Modelling everything "just in case." Modelling is resource-intensive — always ask which of the 5 models actually answers your current elicitation question before building it.
  2. Putting an interactive activity in the system's swimlane. The lane is determined by who performs the activity, not which tools are touched.
  3. Attaching business rules to gateways instead of activities. Correction: rules live on the activity that evaluates the condition, not the diamond.
  4. Confusing Functional Role with Process Role. "Salesclerk" (functional, appears on the org chart) vs. "Requester" (process role, may only exist for the duration of one workflow) —.
  5. Treating "internal/external" in the Resource Model as an ownership question rather than a control/operation question. A paid third-party cloud service (e.g. Workday) is external even though the company pays for and relies on it.
  6. Assuming one universal notation exists. BPMN, UML, and IDEF each cover different models/purposes; Organisation/Location/Business-Rules models are largely tool-defined, not standardised.
  7. Skipping Discovery and going straight to detailed modelling. Discovery deliberately sets context first (in-scope process list, stakeholder roles) before the deeper elicitation interviews happen — most large orgs don't have this context centralised already.
  8. Forgetting that a stakeholder needs an actual activity to earn a swimlane. Being a stakeholder in the Organisation/Resource Model doesn't automatically mean they appear in the Process Workflow Model.
  9. Stating the symptom as the root cause. "Long waiting time" is an issue (the effect). A root cause is the top-level cause behind it — "paper-based process", "late exception check". Rule: do not repeat the issue or symptom as the root cause.
  10. Assuming one issue has one right root cause — or that one root cause fixes one issue. StarMall Issue 2 has four defensible analyses (policy, sequencing, integration), while the paper-based root cause resolves two issues. Grade yourself on a coherent chain issue → cause → root cause, and look for shared root causes across issues.
  11. Reading the RCR scales backwards. Impact: 5 = Very High. Complexity: 5 = Very Easy, 1 = Very Complex. The StarMall answer's "Low Complex" means an easy change. High impact alone doesn't earn top priority — the Real Estate "government policy" recommendation is impact 4 but Very Complex.
  12. Static-report arithmetic slips. (a) Forgetting the input factor, which overstates cost and time for optional tasks (toasting, additional items). (b) Using minutes where the formula needs hours — cost and workload divide by 60. (c) Treating "required resources" (2.03 Veggie Artists) as utilisation; you must divide by resources available (3) → 68%. (d) For nested branches, using only the last gateway's percentage instead of the product of probabilities.
  13. Counting every diamond as a decision. SUBWAY has four diamonds but only two decisions (Toasted?, Additional items?); the other two are merges. Count flows: a decision has several labelled exits, a merge several entries and one exit.
  14. Treating a static report as if it showed waiting. Static analysis has no queues; utilisation of 68% says nothing about how long a customer waits. Waiting, bottlenecks and randomness appear only in dynamic analysis.
  15. Calling the longest task the bottleneck. A bottleneck combines queue length, resource over-utilisation and activity time. Rank by waiting for the resource plus who is over-used, not by execution time alone.
  16. Ranking paths by per-instance cost. Use the expected contribution (share × value). A $97 path at 2.5% contributes $2.44; a $74 path at 45.5% contributes $33.56.
  17. Choosing the "minimum" instead of the "cheapest that meets the goal". In the what-if example the lowest waiting time is 9 servers; the answer to "how many do you need for ≤ 10 min?" is 5.
  18. Presenting To-Be simulation numbers as measured facts. To-Be parameters (new activity times, staffing, arrival rates) are assumed; say so, justify them, and consider sensitivity analysis or Monte Carlo runs. And no single simulation run is "the" answer.
  19. Picking the best-performing To-Be without impact analysis. The best simulated alternative may be infeasible: greater impact → higher risk → higher cost/time → resistance to change. Always consider internal and external, hard and soft impacts.
  20. Business-rule boundary gaps. Rules with < $1000 and > $1000 leave = $1000 undefined. State boundary values and a default outcome.
  21. Turning manual activities into use cases. "MO proceeds to CSC" and "CSO collects booking fee" touch no system, so they produce no use case. Only interactive and automated activities are candidates.
  22. Merging automated use cases. "RAS emails and SMS MO" is two use cases, and a RAS↔IMS hand-off is a client/server pair, one in each system's boundary. The course says "DO NOT combine automated use cases".
  23. Wrong actors. Naming an actor after the person in the scenario (Max → Patient); forgetting actors that have no lane but receive something (the LM, IMS as a system actor); adding the customer when the customer never touches a system.
  24. Packaging across systems. One "Integration" package holding both RAS and IMS use cases, or "Verify UEN" placed in a RAS package. Rule 1: only use cases of the same system can share a package.
  25. Reading change type as "is it manual today?". Change type describes the system: Outlook's Submit Availability is Unchanged although the clinic does it by hand; IMS's Update customer selection is To be modified because it changes from interactive to integrated.
  26. Over-specifying the concept blueprint. Naming the operating system, server vendor or dollar costs. The concept blueprint communicates the vision; cost is a qualitative Low/Med/High with justification.
  27. C4 level confusion. Putting functions/components on the context diagram, or reading "container" as a Docker container. Context = one system box; container = deployable apps and data stores; component = parts of one container.
  28. Risk rating and strategy slips. A is the highest rating; low impact × high likelihood is B, not C. Insurance is transfer, not reduction; "do nothing because alternatives aren't cost-justified" is acceptance. And every mitigation needs its own "impact of strategy".
  29. IoT notation errors. Calling a device's own action a service task (it is a script task), drawing plain sequence arrows between pools (use send tasks and message events), and forgetting the timer start or timer intermediate event.
  30. "Agentic means no humans." Every level of the automation spectrum keeps a human role; agents escalate actions beyond their authority.
  31. Calling every new product "business model innovation". Count the Gassmann corners that change: only What? → product innovation; only How? (value chain) → process innovation; two or more → business model innovation.
  32. Treating invention as innovation. An invention may never be commercialised; innovation is the invention introduced to the marketplace.
  33. Confusing process improvement with process innovation. Improvement optimises an existing process; innovation implements a new or significantly improved method — and radical innovation brings more value, more risk and broader cultural change.
  34. Mixing canvas blocks and triangle corners. Channels and customer relationships belong to Who?, not How?; cost structure belongs to Value? with revenue streams.
  35. Mis-sorting process types. Core = delivers to external customers; support = feeds the core; management = sets direction and rules. Faculty management (core) vs faculty services (support) is the classic trap.
  36. Repeating the Process Executive Model in the Process Hierarchy Model. The Process Hierarchy Model starts at level 3 and goes deeper; the Process Executive Model stops at level 3.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • Structure and reporting → Organisation; who and what is involved → Resource; sequence and interaction → Workflow; decision logic → Business Rules; geography → Location.
  • Qualitative why questions stay static; waiting, alternatives and “how many” need dynamic analysis.
  • Impact 5 is Very High; complexity 5 is Very Easy.
  • Rules attach to activities; lanes follow the performer; count flows to tell decisions from merges.
  • Do not call the longest task the bottleneck.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Which model answers “who is the boss?”tap to flip
Organisation.
Which model answers “what happens next?”tap to flip
Process Workflow.
Which technique answers “how many servers do we need?”tap to flip
What-if analysis.
Static report vs waitingtap to flip
A static report shows no queues; waiting appears only in dynamic analysis.
➡ Where next? You have reached the end: practise with the questions, then take the final exam.

1.q: Which sequence matches the four chapters of the course?
o: Model → Analyse → Solve → Innovate
Analyse → Model → Solve → Innovate
Model → Solve → Analyse → Innovate
Innovate → Model → Analyse → Solve
1.e: The course starts with As-Is models, then analyses them, then specifies solutions, then adds innovation.
w: Analyse needs As-Is models to exist first, so Model comes first.
Solutions are specified for problems already found by analysis, so Solve follows Analyse.
Innovation extends the To-Be design after the process is understood; it is the last chapter.

1.q: Which dimension of business language answers “Why?”
o: Participants
Purpose
Process
Product
1.e: Purpose covers mission, vision and strategic goals, the reason a business exists.
w: Participants answers Who?, the people and systems involved.
Process answers How?, the workflows that deliver value.
Product answers What?, the goods and services delivered.

1.q: Which dimension of business language answers “Who?”
o: Participants
Product
Process
Purpose
1.e: Participants covers every stakeholder, team, customer, system and AI agent, internal and external.
w: Product answers What?, what is delivered.
Process answers How?, the workflows.
Purpose answers Why?, the mission and goals.

1.q: What does the Solve chapter turn the To-Be models into?
o: Simulation parameters
A set of root causes
IT solution requirements
A list of process issues
1.e: Solve expresses the To-Be as functional and non-functional requirements and solutioning models.
w: Simulation parameters belong to dynamic analysis within Analyse.
Root causes are identified in the RCI model during Analyse.
Issues are found in Analyse, from the As-Is.

2.q: Which scope of alignment is delivered through Enterprise Architecture?
o: Technology Alignment
Process Alignment
Project Alignment
Enterprise Alignment
2.e: Enterprise Alignment spans the whole organisation and is delivered via Enterprise Architecture.
w: Technology Alignment is not a scope; it is one of the things being aligned.
Process Alignment is not one of the two scopes of alignment named in the course.
Project Alignment concerns one IT solution and uses the Business Process Engineering Methodology.

2.q: Which BPM cycle phase understands the current state and sets context?
o: Design Solution
Discover
Implement Solution
Monitor & Optimise
2.e: Discover asks what the organisation is actually doing now, deliberately shallowly.
w: Design Solution creates the future solution after analysis.
Implement Solution builds and rolls out the solution.
Monitor & Optimise measures and improves the running process.

2.q: Which statement about a business objective is correct?
o: It is measurable and time-bound
It replaces the mission statement
It describes where the firm wants to be in decades
It is a broad direction with no measure
2.e: Objectives carry numbers and deadlines, which later lets a performance goal be tested.
w: Objectives sit below the mission and vision in the cascade; they do not replace them.
Long-term aspiration is the vision statement's role.
That describes a mission or vision, which is directional rather than measurable.

2.q: Which of these is a root cause of Business–IT misalignment?
o: Too much documentation of strategy
IT staff being paid too much
Lack of a common language between IT and business
Projects finishing early
2.e: Mutual appreciation, shared language and a changing environment drive misalignment.
w: The steps toward alignment include writing strategy down in one document.
Pay levels are not among the stated causes of misalignment.
Early completion is not a cause of misalignment.

3.q: Which phrase completes the course definition: “a repeatable series of activities performed to deliver a service or a product to a…”?
o: supplier
regulator
competitor
stakeholder
3.e: The course definition ends with delivery to a stakeholder.
w: Suppliers provide inputs; they are not the recipient of the outcome in the definition.
Regulators set external rules; the definition delivers the outcome to the stakeholder who receives the service or product.
A competitor does not receive the outcome of the process, so it cannot be the party the definition refers to.

3.q: Which question about a business covers location information?
o: Why?
How?
Where?
Who?
3.e: Where? covers location, such as online or face-to-face.
w: Why? covers strategy, objectives and KPIs.
How? covers workflow and process flow.
Who? covers people and systems.

3.q: Under which of the six questions do business rules sit?
o: When?
What?
Why?
Where?
3.e: When? covers time, business rules and business events.
w: What? covers raw materials, data and products.
Why? covers strategy, objectives and KPIs, not rules.
Where? covers location information.

3.q: Which of these is the atomic unit of a process model?
o: Sub-process
Business process
Activity
Business event
3.e: An activity is a single logical step that is not decomposed further.
w: A sub-process can still be decomposed into further activities.
A business process is made of many activities.
A business event triggers a process; it is not a unit of work.

4.q: Which model is informally known as “People Politics”?
o: Business Rules Model
Organisation Model
Resource Model
Location Model
4.e: It shows relationships between stakeholders in the current organisational context.
w: The Business Rules Model captures rules applied to activities.
The Resource Model lists humans and technology by internal or external.
The Location Model shows geographic distribution.

4.q: Which two models are not among the five studied from the seven views?
o: Organisation and Location
Collaboration and Process Package
Resource and Workflow
Workflow and Business Rules
4.e: The five studied are Organisation, Location, Resource, Process Workflow and Business Rules.
w: Organisation and Location are studied.
Resource and Workflow are studied.
Workflow and Business Rules are studied.

4.q: In the Resource Model, what does “internal” mean?
o: A resource you manage
A resource inside the building
A resource used only by employees
A resource the company pays for
4.e: Internal and external track who controls or operates the resource, not who pays or uses it.
w: Physical location is the Location Model's concern.
Users do not decide internal versus external; control does.
A paid third-party cloud service is still external.

4.q: Which standard time is used for transactions that span time zones?
o: Time at the server's location
Time at the customer's location
Local time at head office
GMT
4.e: The Location Model notes that transactions across time zones use GMT.
w: A server's local time is arbitrary for the other sites; transactions across time zones use GMT so everyone refers to the same instant.
A customer's local time differs between sites, so it cannot give every location the same instant; GMT is the common reference.
Using head-office time would make transactions from other sites ambiguous; the Location Model fixes one common reference, GMT.

5.q: Which activity type is done entirely by a system with no human involvement?
o: Automated
Parallel
Manual
Interactive
5.e: Automated activities sit in the system's lane.
w: Parallel is a gateway behaviour, not an activity type.
Manual is human effort unaided by systems.
Interactive is a human using a system.

5.q: In which lane does an interactive activity belong?
o: The lane of the system used
A lane shared by both
A separate lane for tools
The lane of the human who performs it
5.e: The lane follows who performs the activity, not what they touch.
w: Putting it in the system lane is the common mistake.
A lane belongs to one business participant; the performer owns the activity, so a lane shared by a human and a system does not exist.
Lanes group activities by performer; a tool is only touched by the performer and does not earn a lane of its own.

5.q: What does a dashed arrow in the BPMN legend show?
o: A timer
A work product or association
A merge
A transition
5.e: Dashed or dotted arrows link a document or data object to an activity.
w: A timer is a clock icon on a flow.
A merge is drawn as an unlabelled diamond.
A transition is a solid arrow.

5.q: To what do business rules attach?
o: Start events
Decision gateways
Swimlanes
Activities that evaluate the condition
5.e: The gateway only shows a branch exists; the rule lives with the activity that evaluates it.
w: Start events trigger the process; they hold no rules.
Attaching rules to gateways is the common mistake: the diamond only shows that a branch exists, while the activity evaluating the condition holds the rule.
Swimlanes group activities by participant.

6.q: How are a decision and a merge told apart in the course's diagrams?
o: By the symbol inside the diamond
By counting flows in and out
By the colour of the diamond
By the lane they sit in
6.e: Both can be drawn as an exclusive-gateway diamond, so the number of flows decides.
w: The same marker can appear on both, so the symbol does not decide.
Colour is only styling; the same exclusive-gateway diamond can be a decision or a merge, so you must look at the flows.
Both gateway types can sit in any lane, so lane placement says nothing about whether a diamond is a decision or a merge.

6.q: In the airport check-in diagram, which lane contains the automated activities?
o: Traveler
Check-in Staff
Check-in System
Check-in Counter
6.e: Process booking details and printing the boarding pass and luggage tag are done by the system.
w: The traveller hands over documents manually.
Staff enter booking details, an interactive activity.
There is no lane named Check-in Counter.

6.q: When a task follows two nested branches, how is its input factor found?
o: Add the probabilities on the path
Use only the last gateway's percentage
Average the probabilities on the path
Multiply the probabilities along the path
6.e: The input factor after nested branches is the joint probability, a product.
w: Probabilities of successive branches multiply, not add.
The last gateway alone ignores earlier branches.
Averaging gives a number with no probabilistic meaning.

6.q: Which lane in the order management example contains the only system-performed activity?
o: Sales System
Customer
Sales Agent
Store Keeper
6.e: The Sales System lane holds the email to the Store Keeper, its only activity.
w: The Customer lane holds the order placement and decision.
The Sales Agent lane holds creation and validation of orders.
The Store Keeper lane holds several human activities.

7.q: Which step of static analysis produces the RCI Model?
o: Final Selection
Recommendation Formulation
Issue Elicitation
Issue Analysis
7.e: Issue Analysis quantifies time, cost and workload and explains why each issue exists.
w: Final Selection belongs to dynamic analysis.
Recommendation Formulation produces the RCR Model.
Issue Elicitation produces the Issue List.

7.q: Which of these is an RCI issue category?
o: Technology
Finance
Policy
Culture
7.e: The five categories are Process, System, People, Policy and Others.
w: Technology problems fall under System (IT applications) in the RCI; there is no separate Technology category.
Money-related effects appear as business performance metrics, not as an issue category; the categories describe the type of cause.
Attitudes and skills fall under People; Culture is not a separate RCI category.

7.q: On the RCR complexity scale, what does 5 mean?
o: Very Low
Very Complex
Very High
Very Easy
7.e: Complexity is reversed: 5 is Very Easy and 1 is Very Complex.
w: Very Low is the 1 end of the impact scale; complexity has its own reversed scale where 5 is Very Easy.
Very Complex is the bottom of the complexity scale, which is 1; the scale is reversed so that 5 is the most attractive.
Very High is 5 on the impact scale, not on the complexity scale; there 5 is Very Easy.

7.q: What does cycle time per instance equal in a static report?
o: The longest task time
The probability-weighted sum of task times
The average of task times
The sum of times with no weighting
7.e: Each task time is multiplied by its input factor before summing.
w: The longest task ignores the rest of the path.
A plain average ignores probabilities.
Unweighted sums overstate time for optional tasks.

8.q: Which phase of dynamic analysis identifies who is affected by each To-Be alternative?
o: Model and Simulate
Establish Performance Goals
Impact Analysis
Final Selection
8.e: Phase 3 examines hard/soft and internal/external impacts.
w: Phase 2 produces numbers from simulation.
Phase 1 fixes goals and metrics.
Phase 4 chooses the final To-Be.

8.q: Which data type covers the probability of each decision path?
o: Process-wide
Resource-related
Decision points
Activity-related
8.e: Decision-point data gives the probability of each path from history or assumption.
w: Process-wide data covers triggers and arrival patterns.
Resource-related data covers cost and numbers per role.
Activity-related data covers resources, time and cost per task.

8.q: How many analysis techniques does the course list for the As-Is simulation?
o: Ten
Six
Four
Eight
8.e: Four are listed in the first part (capacity to activities time/cost) and four in the second (bottleneck to what-if).
w: Only eight techniques are listed in two parts of four, so a total of ten would include techniques the course does not name.
The list has two parts of four, so the total is eight; six does not correspond to any grouping in it.
Four is the number in each part; the course lists two parts (capacity to activities, then bottleneck to what-if), giving eight in total.

8.q: Which statement about a bottleneck is correct?
o: It is the task with the longest static time
It is the first activity in the process
It is any activity with a decision gateway
It combines queue length, resource over-use and activity time
8.e: A bottleneck is where work waits for an over-used, scarce resource.
w: The longest task alone is the common mistake.
Position in the flow is irrelevant; a bottleneck is found from queue length, resource over-use and activity time wherever it occurs.
A gateway is only a branch point; a bottleneck arises where work queues for a scarce, over-used resource.

9.q: Which statement describes a functional requirement?
o: What the system should do
How available the system should be
How fast the system should respond
How secure the system should be
9.e: Functional requirements describe behaviour; the others are non-functional qualities.
w: Availability, such as uptime, is a non-functional quality.
Response speed is a performance, non-functional quality.
Security is a non-functional quality.

9.q: What shape is a use case drawn as in a use case diagram?
o: An oval
A stick figure
A solid line
A rectangle containing an actor
9.e: A use case is an oval; actors are stick figures.
w: A stick figure is an actor.
A solid line is an association.
A rectangle is the system boundary.

9.q: How is a manual activity treated when deriving use cases?
o: It becomes a client/server pair
It becomes no use case
It becomes one use case
It becomes an actor
9.e: Manual activities touch no system, so they are not converted.
w: The pair arises for automated activities between two systems.
Interactive activities each yield one use case.
Actors come from lanes and connected systems, not from manual activities.

9.q: Which Function Model change type means the use case is partly supported and needs modification?
o: Unchanged
New (Migrate)
New
To be modified
9.e: To be modified means existing support needs enhancement.
w: Unchanged means fully supported already.
New (Migrate) means moved from another system.
New means it does not exist today.

10.q: Which C4 level shows the system as a single box with its users and connected systems?
o: Code diagram
Container diagram
Context diagram
Component diagram
10.e: The Context diagram zooms out to the big picture.
w: Code zooms into one component.
Container shows the applications and data stores inside the system.
Component zooms into one container.

10.q: Which mitigation strategy shifts the risk to another party?
o: Acceptance
Elimination
Transfer
Reduction
10.e: Transfer, for example through insurance, shifts risk to others.
w: Acceptance does nothing and takes the outcome.
Elimination avoids the risky activity.
Reduction lowers probability or impact.

10.q: Which risk type covers new technology and lack of expertise?
o: Technology risk
Organisational risk
Data risk
Goal risk
10.e: Technology risk includes new technology, lack of expertise and security incidents.
w: Organisational risk concerns resources, roles and departments.
Data risk concerns new or incomplete data.
Goal risk concerns market or policy changes affecting goals.

10.q: In what form does the concept cost model express cost?
o: Hours of effort only
Vendor price quotes
Low, Medium or High
Exact dollar amounts
10.e: It gives a qualitative level with a short justification.
w: Effort hours are one input to cost but the model rates fixed, maintenance and total cost as Low, Med or High.
Vendors and technology are fixed only in the detailed blueprint, so quotes are premature at concept level.
Dollar estimates are the common mistake at concept stage.

11.q: Which corner of the Magic Triangle asks how revenue is created?
o: What?
Value?
Who?
How?
w: What? is the value proposition.
Who? is the customer segment.
How? is the value chain.

11.q: Which Business Model Canvas block maps to the How? corner?
o: Customer Relationships
Value Proposition
Revenue Streams
Key Activities
11.e: Key Resources, Key Activities and Key Partners form How?.
w: Customer Relationships belong to Who?.
Value Proposition belongs to What?.
Revenue Streams belong to Value?.

11.q: A change to only the value chain is which type of innovation?
o: Process innovation
Product innovation
Incremental invention
Business model innovation
11.e: Process innovation changes only How?, the value chain.
w: Product innovation changes only What?.
Incremental invention is not one of the three types; the three are product, process and business model innovation.
Business model innovation changes two or more corners.

11.q: How does innovation differ from invention?
o: Innovation precedes invention
Innovation commercialises an invention
Innovation needs no organisational change
Innovation is limited to R&D
11.e: Invention creates something new; innovation introduces it to the market.
w: Invention precedes innovation.
Innovation brings organisational change.
Innovation spreads across the organisation; R&D is where invention is usually restricted.

12.q: Which automation level selects its process path dynamically?
o: Agentic automation
Traditional digital automation
Intelligent automation
Robotic process automation
12.e: Agentic automation chooses its path dynamically, governed by goals, policies and constraints.
w: Traditional digital automation has a predefined path.
Intelligent automation has a mostly predefined path.
RPA follows a predefined path through the user interface.

12.q: Which is the least automated level of IoT use?
o: Control
Monitor
Predict
Alert
12.e: At Monitor a human observes the displayed information.
w: Control changes the environment through a system or actuator.
Predict recommends an intervention.
Alert notifies a person or creates a task.

12.q: Which BPMN task models an IoT device performing its own hardware function?
o: Service task
Script task
Send task
User task
12.e: A script task is executed by the process engine, such as a sensor reading humidity.
w: A service task is a control system calling a device or service.
A send task sends a message to another pool.
A user task is a human using a software application.

12.q: Which of these is an IoT challenge named in the course?
o: Usability
Scalability
Compatibility
Profitability
12.e: The four challenges are Security, Privacy, Connectivity and Compatibility.
w: Usability concerns user interfaces and is not among the four challenges the course names for IoT.
Scalability is not one of the four named challenges, which are security, privacy, connectivity and compatibility.
Profitability is a business outcome; the four named challenges are security, privacy, connectivity and compatibility.

13.q: Which type of process produces the products or services delivered to external customers?
o: Management process
Core process
Supporting process
Sub-process
13.e: Core processes embody critical expertise and serve external customers.
w: Management processes direct and control.
Supporting processes feed core processes.
A sub-process is a smaller process within another.

13.q: How many levels does the Process Executive Model usually show?
o: One
Seven or more
Four to six
Two to three
13.e: The Process Executive Model stops at level 3; deeper levels are in hierarchy models.
w: A single level could not show sub-processes; the Process Executive Model shows two to three levels.
Seven or more levels would make the diagram too complex; the Process Executive Model stops at level 3 and deeper levels go in hierarchy models.
Four to six levels belong in hierarchy models.

13.q: Which framework is cross-industry rather than industry-specific?
o: SCOR
SAP Business Maps
APQC PCF
eTOM
13.e: The Process Classification Framework spans industries.
w: SCOR is for supply chain management.
SAP Business Maps are organised by industry.
eTOM is for telecoms.

13.q: Which are the three components of a process architecture?
o: Value, risk and levels
Actors, use cases and packages
Processes, risks and costs
Functional units, processes and levels
13.e: Both models are built from functional units, processes and levels.
w: Value and risk are not components of process architecture.
Actors, use cases and packages belong to functional requirements.
Risk and cost belong to the blueprint.

14.q: Which model best answers “Who is the boss?”
o: Resource Model
Organisation Model
Business Rules Model
Process Workflow Model
14.e: Structure and reporting questions go to the Organisation Model.
w: The Resource Model lists who and what is involved.
The Business Rules Model covers decision logic.
The Process Workflow Model covers sequence and interaction.

14.q: Which model best answers “How do you decide on the discount amount?”
o: Location Model
Organisation Model
Business Rules Model
Resource Model
14.e: Decision logic goes to the Business Rules Model.
w: Location covers geography.
Organisation covers structure.
Resource lists who and what is involved.

14.q: Which technique answers “How many staff do we need to hit a goal?”
o: RCI model
What-if analysis
Static report
Path analysis
14.e: Questions about alternatives and resource numbers need dynamic what-if analysis.
w: RCI explains why issues exist.
A static report gives cycle time and cost.
Path analysis compares paths and their expected contribution.

14.q: Which C4 diagram answers “What is in scope and which outside systems does it talk to?”
o: Context diagram
Component diagram
Code diagram
Container diagram
14.e: The Context diagram shows the system, its users and connected systems.
w: The Component diagram shows internals of one container.
The Code diagram shows code elements.
The Container diagram shows deployable applications and data stores.
